Soemmerring's gazelle (Nanger soemmerringii) is a large-bodied antelope inhabiting the arid and semi-arid grasslands of the Horn of Africa, where it exhibits a life history strategy finely tuned to unpredictable resource availability. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of approximately 40 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 40 kilograms], a size that places them among the heavier members of the gazelle tribe. Newborn calves weigh around 5100 grams [Wwb = around 5100 grams] at birth, a neonatal mass that represents a substantial maternal investment relative to the adult female mass. This precocial neonate is able to stand and follow its mother within hours of parturition, an adaptation to the open, predator-rich habitats the species occupies. The initial period of rapid mass gain is supported entirely by the mother's milk, and the suckling juvenile remains dependent on her for several months. Field records indicate that the time since birth at weaning is approximately 100 days [tx = approximately 100 days], a duration that allows the calf to achieve a body mass of about 15000 grams [Wwx = about 15000 grams] before transitioning to an exclusively herbivor at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]ous diet. This period of nutritional dependence is relatively short for a bovid of this size, presumably reflecting the selective pressure to minimize the window of vulnerability to predation.

Reproductive output in Soemmerring's gazelle is relatively modest, consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of large ungulates in unpredictable environments. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic state (38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate is achieved when a single calf is born each year, with females producing one calf per birth event [N_R_i = one calf per birth event] and one litter annually [F_R_i = one litter annually]. This slow reproductive schedule is enforced in part by a gestation period that extends for 270 days [tg = 270 days] at the same core body temperature, a duration that is significantly longer than the 150-160 day gestation reported in the literature for some other gazelles from the same genus at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. The extended gestation likely reflects the evolutionary pressure to deliver a relatively large, well-developed precocial calf capable of escaping predators shortly after birth. Consequently, females cannot accelerate their reproductive output beyond this single annual event, even during periods of exceptional forage abundance. This life-history constraint shapes the overall population dynamics of the species, limiting its maximum potential rate of increase even under favorable ecological conditions.

The developmental trajectory from birth to reproductive maturity spans a considerable portion of the species' lifespan. Puberty is attained at 640 days since birth [tp = 640 days since birth] when the core body temperature measures 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], marking the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for gamete production. This relatively late sexual maturation is consistent with the species' investment in a large adult body size and the extended period of somatic growth required to reach the approximately 40 kilogram asymptote characteristic of females. The intervening juvenile and sub-adult phases are characterized by a steady increase in body mass and the gradual development of the skeletal and muscular systems needed for the strenuous male-male combat that occurs during the breeding season. Males typically reach sexual maturity slightly later than females, a common pattern among polygynous ungulates where body size and fighting ability are key determinants of reproductive success. The prolonged period between birth and the first successful copulation represents a significant demographic cost, as individuals must survive multiple years of exposure to predation and environmental stochasticity before they can contribute genetically to the next generation. This extended pre-receptive period is a hallmark of the species' conservative life-history strategy. The maximum reproductive output, which amounts to a single calf per year [Ri = single calf per year], reinforces this pattern of slow growth and late maturation.

Longevity records for this antelope indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15.5 years [am = approximately 15.5 years] when individuals are maintained at a stable core temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], a value that has been documented through long-term monitoring of both wild and captive populations. This lifespan is substantial for a medium-sized bovid and reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates experienced by adults in their natural habitat once they reach full body size. The age-related decline in physiological function, or senescence, becomes apparent in the final years of life, with older individuals showing reduced muscle mass, worn dentition, and declining reproductive output. The trade-off between the investment in a single, high-quality calf each year and the extended lifespan is a classic example of the slow-fast continuum in life-history evolution. Comparative data from related antelope species suggest that this longevity is near the upper end of expectations for a 40-kilogram mammal, underscoring the conservative pace of life in this arid-adapted grazer. The combination of late maturity, low annual fecundity, and a long reproductive lifespan allows populations to buffer against occasional catastrophic droughts.

Basal metabolic rate in Soemmerring's gazelle has been quantified through respirometry trials on adults that had attained their ultimate body mass of approximately 40 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 40 kilograms]. The maximum resting oxygen consumption was measured at 9213 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 9213 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animal's core temperature was maintained at the physiologically normal level of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. This metabolic rate, which is based on a body mass of 35,100 grams for the measured individuals, is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships observed across the Bovidae. The relatively modest metabolic demand reflects the species' adaptation to a low-quality, high-fiber diet of dry grasses and forbs, which requires a slow passage rate through the ruminant digestive system. The measured oxygen consumption supports the energetic requirements of a 40-kilogram female throughout the annual cycle, including the costly periods of late gestation and early lactation. This physiological baseline provides the energetic foundation upon which all other life-history traits are built, from the daily foraging itineraries to the long-term investment in a single, large calf each breeding season.
